issues.issue: Article 1's rule that this Agreement governs any inconsistency in the other Contract Documents cannot be squared with Supplementary Condition 1.2.1.1, which resolves inconsistencies within or between Contract Documents by requiring the better quality/greater quantity per the Architect's interpretation. The two supply different precedence rules for the same problem.

"The relationship of trust and confidence established by this Agreement" is capable of being read either as ordinary contractual cooperation language or as creating fiduciary duties owed by the Contractor to the Owner. The clause gives no definition or limit for that phrase.

The commencement date is fixed only as "Approximately the Fifteenth of July, Two Thousand Two," and "approximately" leaves the date from which the Contract Time runs indeterminate. The default rule (date of the Agreement) and the inserted approximate date point to different dates.

The completion deadline is stated as "five hundred [blank] calendar days from the date of commencement," so the number of days actually agreed cannot be read off the provision. The alternative "or as follows" slot is empty.

This day-count deadline conflicts with Article 4.3 as revised by the First Addendum, which fixes Substantial Completion at the calendar date November 30, 2003. Which measure controls the Contract Time is not stated here.

Defining the Contract Sum as the open-ended Cost of the Work plus the Fee sits badly with Subparagraph 5.2.1, where the Guaranteed Maximum Price is filled in as "N/A," and with A201 9.1.1, which says the Contract Sum "is stated in the Agreement." No stated or capped sum exists anywhere in the instrument.

The operative guarantee reads "not to exceed N/A Dollars ($ N/A)" — the number that makes the guarantee mean anything is absent, so the sentence that follows (costs exceeding the GMP are borne by the Contractor) has no content. That is a writing error that changes what the provision does.

A GMP of "N/A" cannot be reconciled with the many provisions that operate on a real GMP figure — 8.1.8 (costs exceeding the GMP not reimbursed), 12.1.5 (schedule of values allocates "the entire Guaranteed Maximum Price"), 12.1.6, 12.1.7.1, 12.2.5 and 13.2. Read as a whole, the instrument both is and is not a guaranteed-maximum-price contract.

The allowance slot is left blank, yet A201 3.8.2 and 3.8.3 set out a detailed regime for adjusting the Contract Sum when costs differ from "stated allowance amounts." Whether any allowances exist is left unresolved.
The clause governs "adjustments to the Guaranteed Maximum Price," but 5.2.1 fills the GMP in as "N/A," so there is nothing to adjust. The change-order machinery has no price to operate on.

The provision defines "fee" by reference to "the Contractor's Fee as defined in Subparagraph 5.1.1," but the Contractor's Fee is stated in Subparagraph 5.1.2; 5.1.1 defines the Contract Sum. The cross-reference is mistaken.
"Substantial inequity to the Owner or Contractor" and "equitably adjusted" set no standard by which the adjustment of the Fee is to be measured. The trigger and the remedy are both left at large.

"Costs necessarily incurred by the Contractor in the proper performance of the Work" and "rates not higher than the standard paid at the place of the Project" are the operative limits on reimbursement, and both are undefined and contestable on any given invoice. In a cost-plus contract this is the phrase the parties fight over.

The blank in 7.2.2 for home-office personnel is unfilled while 8.1.1 excludes such personnel "except as specifically provided in Subparagraphs 7.2.2 and 7.2.3 or as may be provided in Article 14," and the First Addendum's revised 8.1.8 says the Fee covers senior management and administrative support. Whether any office personnel are reimbursable is left contradictory.
"Reasonable waste and spoilage" sets no measurable boundary on how much excess material may be charged to the Owner. The provision offers no benchmark for reasonableness.

Subparagraph 7.5.1 makes hand tools "not customarily owned by construction workers" a reimbursable Cost of the Work, while Exhibit C provides that the cost of all such hand tools "shall be borne by the Contractor" and substitutes a flat 5% payroll add-on. The two cannot both govern the same items.

Subparagraph 7.6.1 reimburses only "that portion of insurance and bond premiums that can be directly attributed to this Contract," whereas Exhibit D fixes the general liability premium at a flat 1% of labor and subcontractor costs. Actual attribution and the flat formula will not produce the same number.

Subparagraphs 7.7.2 and 7.7.3 as printed here are both rewritten by the First Addendum's revised 7.7.2 and 7.7.3, which add exclusions for conditions caused by the Contractor and for lapsed insurance. Both versions appear in the instrument.

Subparagraph 8.1.8 here excludes costs that would cause the Guaranteed Maximum Price to be exceeded, but the First Addendum replaces 8.1.8 entirely with a provision about what the Contractor's Fee covers, and 5.2.1 states the GMP as "N/A." The exclusion in this text has been displaced and has no referent.

"Those portions of the Work that the Contractor does not customarily perform with the Contractor's own personnel" fixes the boundary of what must be subcontracted by reference to an unstated custom. What the Contractor "customarily" self-performs is nowhere defined.
The remedy is a Change Order adjusting the Guaranteed Maximum Price, but 5.2.1 sets the GMP at "N/A." There is no GMP for this adjustment mechanism to operate on.

The payment mechanism turns on filled-in blanks — application received "not later than the [blank] day of a month," payment "not later than the [blank] day of the following month," otherwise within "[blank] days" — and those figures are not legible in the executed text. The timing of the Owner's payment obligation therefore cannot be fixed from the words.

"Any other evidence required by the Owner or Architect" is an open-ended add-on to a specific list of payroll, petty cash and receipted invoices, leaving the Contractor's documentation obligation without a boundary. Whether a demanded document is within the clause is a matter of construction.

The schedule of values "shall allocate the entire Guaranteed Maximum Price among the various portions of the Work," but 5.2.1 states the GMP as "N/A." There is no sum to allocate, so the basis for reviewing Applications for Payment is left undefined.

The percentage-of-completion formula divides by "the share of the Guaranteed Maximum Price allocated to that portion of the Work," a figure that cannot exist because 5.2.1 fixes the GMP as "N/A." The second limb of the test is inoperable.

Each progress payment is computed from "that portion of the Guaranteed Maximum Price properly allocable to completed Work," yet 5.2.1 states the GMP as "N/A." The core payment computation has no input.
The retainage figure is written as "N/A percent (N/A %)," so the clause states a deduction of an unspecified amount. As drafted it neither imposes retainage nor waives it.
The First Addendum's revised Clause 12.1.7.3 sets retainage on the Fee at five percent (5%), directly contradicting the "N/A percent" in this text. Both versions sit in the instrument.

This subparagraph is numbered 12.1.9, the same number carried by the immediately following provision on the Architect's reliance, so cross-references to "12.1.9" are indeterminate. That is a numbering error visible on the face of the text.

The conditions of final payment stated here are supplemented by the First Addendum's new Clause 12.2.1.3 (recorded Notice of Completion) and altered in timing by revised 12.2.2. Whether the Architect's final Certificate remains a precondition when the Addendum's earlier trigger arrives is unresolved.

The 30-day-after-final-Certificate deadline is displaced by the First Addendum's revised 12.2.2, which measures final payment from recordation of the Notice of Completion or a lien-free title endorsement, "whichever is earlier." The two timing rules cannot both apply.

This clause lets the Contractor demand arbitration of the final accounting "without a further decision of the Architect," while A201 4.4.1 makes an initial decision of the Architect a condition precedent to arbitration of Claims. The interaction of the two routes is not spelled out.

Reimbursement is capped at the Guaranteed Maximum Price and the clause assumes savings participation "as provided in Paragraph 5.2," but 5.2.1 states the GMP as "N/A" and the savings-participation slot was left blank. Both premises of the clause are absent from the instrument.
The cap on termination-for-cause payment is that it "shall not cause the Guaranteed Maximum Price to be exceeded," but 5.2.1 fills the GMP in as "N/A." The first limb of the cap is inoperable.
Suspension is to increase "the Guaranteed Maximum Price and Contract Time," but 5.2.1 states the GMP as "N/A," so only the time limb can operate. The price relief promised here has no referent.

No interest rate was inserted, so the clause falls back on "the legal rate prevailing from time to time at the place where the Project is located," a phrase that does not identify which statutory or judgment rate is meant. The rate payable on unpaid sums is therefore left to construction.

This names "Mr. or Mrs. Paul Stephens or Mary Williamson" as the Owner's representative, while Supplementary Condition 2.1.1.1 names Mary Williamson as "the Owner's authorized representative" and then permits action by Paul Stephens, Elle M. Stephens or Mary Williamson. A201 2.1.1 contemplates a single representative with express authority to bind.

This enumeration is superseded by the First Addendum's revised 15.1.1, which defines the Agreement as the A111 "as modified by the First Addendum hereto." The unrevised text omits the Addendum from the enumerated documents.

The Addendum recites that the Agreement was "dated February 1, 2002," while the Agreement's own date line is incomplete and the printed AIA form was generated later in 2002. Because Article 4.1 makes the date of the Agreement the default date of commencement, the discrepancy matters.

"Only skilled and properly trained staff" states a quality standard with no definition or measure, and the sentence has no stated consequence for breach. What counts as "properly trained" is left open.

The sentence begins without a subject ("designate one appropriately skilled and experienced supervisory employee"), and the qualifier that the employee may take other work "only to the extent it does not impair his or her ability to perform this Work" sets no measurable limit. Both the grammar and the standard are open.

It is not stated whether this single supervisory employee is the "competent superintendent" A201 3.9.1 requires to be in attendance at the site during performance, or an additional person. The two requirements overlap without being reconciled.

"The date of commencement of the work shall be July 15, 2002, pending approval of permits" does not say what happens if permits are not approved by that date — whether commencement (and hence the Contract Time) slides. "Pending" carries both a conditional and a merely temporal reading.

A commencement date contingent on permits sits awkwardly with revised 4.3, which fixes Substantial Completion at the fixed calendar date November 30, 2003 rather than at a period running from commencement. A delay in permits shortens the Contract Time with no stated adjustment.

The Owner promises a bonus of "a sum to be determined" for early completion, with the sum "divided between the key management staff, as determined by the Owner" — neither the amount, the formula, nor the identity of the recipients is fixed. As written the obligation may be an unenforceable agreement to agree or a wholly discretionary payment.

The Preliminary Budget is defined only as the Contractor's "current best estimate of the Contract Sum, based on industry-standard figures and the Preliminary Drawings," and the clause never says whether the estimate binds the Contractor on price. "Industry-standard figures" is itself an undefined benchmark.

Whether this budget caps the Owner's exposure cannot be settled against 5.1.1 (Contract Sum is the Cost of the Work plus the Fee) and 5.2.1 (Guaranteed Maximum Price "N/A"), which leave the price open-ended. The Addendum introduces a budget into a contract with no price ceiling.

The direction that a Change Order "shall be issued to adjust the Contract Sum" as Schedule of Values prices are refined cannot be squared with 5.1.1, under which the Contract Sum is simply the Cost of the Work plus the Fee and is not a figure fixed in advance to be adjusted. It also assumes a settled Contract Sum that 5.2.1 (GMP "N/A") does not supply.

The carve-out for emergency costs "capable of being prevented through timely notice of an unsafe condition to Owner or Architect" turns reimbursement on an unmeasured hypothetical about what notice would have prevented. "Capable of being prevented" has no stated boundary.

This revision provides that the Fee covers "all main office expenses including telephone, postage, supplies, facsimiles, stationery" and that none of the listed items is directly reimbursable under Article 7, while Article 7.5.4 makes document reproductions, facsimile transmissions, long-distance calls and postage reimbursable Costs of the Work. It also replaces the original 8.1.8 cap on costs exceeding the Guaranteed Maximum Price, leaving no such cap.

Subsection (c) — "such other information, documentation, and material as Owner or the Architect reasonably may require" — is an open catch-all following two carefully specified items, so the reach of the payment-application conditions is uncertain. Whether a demanded item falls within (c) is a question of construction.

Final payment is due 50 days after recordation of the Notice of Completion or 5 business days after a lien-free title endorsement, "whichever is earlier," but the two triggers may occur in either order and one may never occur at all. The clause does not say what happens if the endorsement is never obtained.

This timing rule can make final payment fall due before the Architect issues the final Certificate for Payment, which 12.2.1 and A201 9.10.1 make a condition of final payment. The two conditions are not reconciled.

This names "Mr. or Mrs. Paul Stephens or Mary Williamson" as the Owner's representative, while Supplementary Condition 2.1.1.1 designates Mary Williamson as the authorized representative and separately allows Paul Stephens, Elle M. Stephens or Mary Williamson to act. Who can bind the Owner is left inconsistent.

The sentence says that when a provision of the General Conditions "is modified or deleted by these Supplementary Conditions, the unaltered provision of the General Conditions shall remain in effect" — read literally the deleted or modified provision survives, which would undo every supplement. The intended reading (unaltered portions remain) is not what the words say.

Requiring the Owner's express written concurrence wherever the Architect's approval is called for cuts across A201 4.2.13, which makes the Architect's decisions on aesthetic effect final, and A201 4.2.1, under which the Architect administers the Contract as the Owner's representative. Whose approval controls is left uncertain.

The instruction to "provide the better quality or greater quantity of Work" or "comply with the more stringent requirement" gives no measure for comparing quality or stringency, and says nothing about price adjustment for the more expensive alternative. The Contractor's obligation on any inconsistency is therefore indeterminate.

This inconsistency rule contradicts Article 1 of the Agreement, which provides that where anything in the other Contract Documents is inconsistent with the Agreement, the Agreement governs. Two different tie-breakers apply to the same conflict.

The flat bar on "extra charge or compensation ... on account of differences between actual dimensions and the dimensions indicated on the Drawings" is hard to reconcile with A201 4.3.4, which gives an equitable adjustment for concealed or unknown site conditions differing materially from the Contract Documents. The overlap between dimensional differences and differing conditions is unaddressed.

The clause designates Mary Williamson as "the Owner's authorized representative" and then permits binding action by Paul Stephens, Elle M. Stephens or Mary Williamson, while revised Article 14.3 names "Mr. or Mrs. Paul Stephens or Mary Williamson" and A201 2.1.1 contemplates one representative with express authority to bind. The instrument gives three inconsistent answers to who speaks for the Owner.

This revision lets the Owner self-correct after a single seven-day notice, whereas A201 2.4.1 as printed in the incorporated General Conditions requires a second seven-day written notice before the Owner may act. Both texts appear in the Contract Documents.

Deeming the evolving Construction Schedule "attached to Document A111 as a part of the Contract Documents" is difficult to square with A201 3.10.1, under which the Contractor's schedule shall not exceed time limits current under the Contract Documents, and with revised 4.3's fixed completion date. A unilaterally updated schedule would become a contract term overriding the agreed date.

Providing that each phase cost estimate "shall become part of the Contract Documents" leaves it unclear whether those estimates bind the price, which 5.1.1 defines as the Cost of the Work plus the Fee with no maximum (5.2.1 being "N/A"), and which Supplementary Condition 7.1.3.1 says may be changed only by Change Order.

The clause is numbered 4.3.1.4 although it plainly belongs with the time-claim provisions at 4.3.7, and the operative sentence ("a separate increase in the Contract Time for each one of the number of causes of delay") is garbled. Its reach over concurrent delay is not clear from the words.

The absolute bar on claims founded on course of conduct, acceptance of extra work or unjust enrichment is in tension with the Addendum's own Section 6.5 and 3.10.5, under which the price is refined through evolving budgets and estimates that "become part of the Contract Documents" without a signed Change Order for each refinement.

Making agreement on a Change Order a "final settlement of all matters relating to the change ... including all direct and indirect costs" and adjustments to the Construction Schedule leaves open whether it waives later cumulative-impact and delay claims arising from that change. The scope of "indirect costs" is undefined.

The provision says in one sentence that the cost of all hand tools not customarily owned by construction workers "shall be borne by the Contractor" and in the next that a flat 5% is added to payroll costs to cover those same tools, which makes the Owner pay for them. The two sentences contradict each other about who bears the cost.

The 5% flat charge cannot be reconciled with Subparagraph 7.5.1, which reimburses hand tools not customarily owned by workers at actual cost less salvage value, or with 7.5.2, under which rental rates and quantities of equipment require the Owner's prior approval. The listed items (air compressors, beam saws, pneumatic nailers) straddle both regimes.

Rental rates for the Contractor's own equipment are fixed by an Equipment Rate Sheet "based upon standard rates paid at the place of the Project," whereas 7.5.2 requires the Owner's prior approval of rates and quantities of rented equipment. The Exhibit sets the rates that 7.5.2 makes subject to approval.

Billing the general liability premium at a flat 1% of labor and subcontractor costs conflicts with Subparagraph 7.6.1, which reimburses only "that portion of insurance and bond premiums that can be directly attributed to this Contract." A formulaic percentage and actual attribution will not match.

The exhibit defines exempt "Subcontract" costs to include "certain vendors' costs" and then gives an open list ending in "etc.," so which vendor charges escape the general excise tax add-on cannot be determined. The catch-all sits directly against the enumerated examples.

The statement that the Contract "may be amended or modified only by Modification" is hard to square with the Addendum's Section 3.10.5, under which evolving cost estimates and schedules "become part of the Contract Documents" without a signed Modification. The instrument both closes and opens the route to amendment.

Performance is required "only to the extent consistent with the Contract Documents and reasonably inferable from them as being necessary to produce the indicated results" — the phrase "reasonably inferable" is the boundary of the Contractor's scope and is nowhere defined. Scope disputes turn on exactly that wording.

This requires the Owner to designate one representative "who shall have express authority to bind the Owner," while Supplementary Condition 2.1.1.1 names Mary Williamson yet allows three individuals to act, and revised 14.3 names a different combination. The instrument does not settle who holds binding authority.

The text of this subparagraph is broken and incomplete — the obligation, the fifteen-day period and the subject of the required information run together without a coherent sentence. What the Owner must furnish, and when, cannot be read off the words.

"Reasonable evidence that financial arrangements have been made to fulfill the Owner's obligations" is undefined, yet furnishing it is made a condition precedent to commencement or continuation of the Work and its absence supports termination under 14.1.1.4. What suffices as reasonable evidence is left entirely open.

This two-notice procedure is displaced by Supplementary Condition 2.4.1 [Revision], which allows the Owner to correct after a single seven-day notice. Both versions appear in the Contract Documents with no statement of which prevails other than the general supplement rule.

The clause both requires the Contractor to "carefully study and compare" the documents and says the review is "not for the purpose of discovering errors, omissions, or inconsistencies," while still requiring prompt report of any discovered. The extent of the Contractor's review duty is left in tension within a single sentence.

The Contractor is excused from liability for document errors "unless the Contractor recognized such error, inconsistency or omission and knowingly failed to report it" — a state-of-mind test with no objective content, in a passage whose text is partly garbled. The line between excused and liable is not drawn.

This fragment of the warranty provision omits the operative warranty itself and begins mid-sentence, while carving out "improper or insufficient maintenance, improper operation, or normal wear and tear and normal usage." What is warranted, and for how long, cannot be determined from the text as it appears.

This makes the Contractor pay sales, consumer, use and similar taxes, while Subparagraph 7.6.2 of the Agreement makes such taxes a reimbursable Cost of the Work and Exhibit D includes the Hawaii general excise tax "as a job cost" calculated on all direct costs. Who ultimately bears the tax is answered differently in the two places.
"Shall assume appropriate responsibility for such Work" states a consequence without saying what responsibility is appropriate or how it is measured. The clause leaves its own remedy undefined.

The allowance adjustment machinery presupposes "stated allowance amounts," but Subparagraph 5.2.4 of the Agreement leaves the allowances slot blank. There are no allowances for this provision to operate on.

The requirement of a competent superintendent in attendance at the site overlaps the Addendum's revised Article 2, which requires one designated supervisory employee who may take other work. Whether these are the same person, and whether the superintendent may work elsewhere, is unresolved.

This schedule provision, which forbids a schedule exceeding time limits current under the Contract Documents, sits against the Addendum's 3.10.4 and 3.10.5, which make the updated Construction Schedule itself part of the Contract Documents. Which controls the completion obligation is not stated.
"In general accordance with the most recent schedules submitted" gives no measurable standard of schedule compliance. Whether a lagging Contractor is in breach turns entirely on that phrase.

The Contractor's duty to pay all royalties and license fees here overlaps Subparagraph 7.6.5 of the Agreement, which makes such royalties, license fees and defence costs reimbursable Costs of the Work in some circumstances and excluded in others. Which regime governs a given royalty is not settled.

The indemnity applies "to the fullest extent permitted by law" and "only to the extent caused by the negligent acts or omissions" of the Contractor, yet also applies "regardless of whether or not such claim ... is caused in part by a party indemnified hereunder." The extent of the Owner's own-negligence coverage is left to construction.

Routing communications through the Architect is difficult to reconcile with Supplementary Condition 1.1.2.1, which requires notice to and the express written consent of the Owner wherever the Architect's is required. The two set different channels for the same communications.

The provision survives only as a fragment — the Architect's obligation to review Applications for Payment and certify amounts due is broken into disconnected phrases. What the Architect must do cannot be read off the text.

"Matters relating to aesthetic effect" is undefined but carries heavy consequences, since Claims relating to aesthetic effect are excluded from mediation and arbitration under 4.5.1 and 4.6.1. Whether a workmanship or finish complaint is an aesthetic matter is left open.

The finality of the Architect's aesthetic decisions is hard to reconcile with Supplementary Condition 1.1.2.1, by which the Owner reserves approval rights "for purposes of aesthetic and cost control of the Work." Both the Architect and the Owner are given the last word on aesthetics.

Claims must be initiated within 21 days of the event "or within 21 days after the claimant first recognizes the condition giving rise to the Claim, whichever is later," but the provision states no consequence for missing the period. Whether late notice bars the Claim turns on words that do not say so.

Relief turns on conditions that "differ materially" from those indicated, or unknown conditions "of an unusual nature" differing materially from those ordinarily found, none of which is defined or measured. Whether a given site condition qualifies is a pure question of construction.

The clause lists six specific grounds for additional-cost claims and then adds "(7) other reasonable grounds," leaving the reach of the catch-all uncertain against the enumerated specifics. Whether it is confined to grounds of the same kind is exactly the ejusdem generis question.

Weather claims require data showing conditions were "abnormal for the period of time, could not have been reasonably anticipated and had an adverse effect," with no baseline stated for abnormality. On a Hawaii project the benchmark is left entirely open.

The provision operates on "unit prices stated in the Contract Documents," but Subparagraph 5.2.3 of the Agreement leaves the unit-price slot blank. There are no unit prices for the equitable-adjustment mechanism to apply to.

The mutual waiver of "consequential damages" is followed by illustrative lists and a saving for "liquidated direct damages," leaving the line between waived consequential loss and recoverable direct loss undrawn. Which side of the line delay or completion costs fall on is a construction question.

The waiver is said to apply "without limitation, to all consequential damages due to either party's termination in accordance with Article 14," yet 14.1.3 lets a terminating Contractor recover "reasonable overhead, profit and damages" and 14.4.3 allows overhead and profit on Work not executed. The two provisions pull in opposite directions on termination recovery.

The Architect's initial decision is made "a condition precedent to mediation, arbitration or litigation of all Claims ... unless 30 days have passed after the Claim has been referred to the Architect with no decision having been rendered." Whether a party that never referred a Claim is barred, and how the proviso interacts with the bar, is left to construction.

This condition precedent sits against Subparagraph 12.2.4 of the Agreement, which lets the Contractor demand arbitration of the final accounting "without a further decision of the Architect." The instrument gives two different routes to arbitration.

The Architect's approval or rejection of a Claim is stated to be "final and binding on the parties but subject to mediation and arbitration," which are two inconsistent characterisations in one sentence. What the decision binds, and to what effect in a later proceeding, is unclear.

The 30-day demand rule operates only when the Architect's written decision "states" both of two things, and the consequence of failing to demand within 30 days — the decision becoming final and binding — is expressed in text that is partly broken here. Whether a decision triggered the deadline is left to construction.

Mediation is made "a condition precedent to arbitration or the institution of legal or equitable proceedings," subject to exceptions for aesthetic effect and waived Claims, with the Architect's decision or 30 days' delay as the starting point. Whether suit is barred by a failure to mediate, and which Claims escape, are both live on these words.

The arbitration agreement covers "any Claim arising out of or related to the Contract" except aesthetic-effect Claims and those waived under 4.3.10, 9.10.4 and 9.10.5, and is conditioned on the Architect's initial decision or 30 days' delay. The scope of the exceptions and the effect of the condition are the classic points of dispute, and the text here is partly garbled.

The outer limit is the date when "institution of legal or equitable proceedings based on such Claim would be barred by the applicable statute of limitations as determined pursuant to Paragraph 13.7," which requires layering a contractual accrual rule onto a statutory period. When a demand is too late is not readable from the clause alone.

Joinder is permitted only of persons "substantially involved in a common question of fact or law whose presence is required if complete relief is to be accorded," and excluded where the interest or responsibility is "insubstantial." Both tests are undefined and decide who may be brought into the arbitration.

The demanding party "must assert in the demand all Claims then known to that party," but the provision states no consequence for omitting one. Whether omitted Claims are waived is not answered by the words.

The Architect-and-Owner approval route for proposed subcontractors overlaps Article 10.1 of the Agreement, under which the Contractor delivers bids and "the Owner shall then determine, with the advice of the Contractor and the Architect, which bids will be accepted." Two different selection procedures are provided.

A Change Order is defined as an instrument signed by Owner, Contractor and Architect, while the Addendum's Section 6.5 says a Change Order "shall be issued" whenever a Schedule of Values price is refined and 3.10.5 makes revised estimates part of the Contract Documents without signature. The formalities do not match.

The subparagraph survives only as a broken fragment ("determining adjustments to the Contract Sum may include those listed"), so the methods it refers to cannot be identified from the text. What it provides is unreadable.

The Architect must fix the adjustment "on the basis of reasonable expenditures and savings," and the enumerated cost categories close with "additional costs of supervision and field office personnel directly attributable to the change." Both the reasonableness standard and the closed list's reach are open to argument.

The Architect's power to order minor changes binding on the Owner is in tension with Supplementary Condition 1.2.1.1(c), which requires Owner and Architect approval of minor field changes, and with 1.1.2.1, which requires the Owner's express written concurrence wherever the Architect acts. Whether the Architect alone can bind the Owner is unsettled.

Contract Time is defined as a "period of time ... allotted in the Contract Documents" for Substantial Completion, but revised Article 4.3 fixes completion by a calendar date rather than a period, and original 4.3's day-count is incomplete. The measure of the Contract Time is not consistently expressed.

This treats the date of commencement as "the date established in the Agreement," while Article 4.1 gives only an approximate July date and revised 4.1 makes it July 15, 2002 "pending approval of permits." No single established date exists.

After enumerating specific delay causes the clause adds "other causes beyond the Contractor's control" and "other causes which the Architect determines may justify delay," so the reach of the catch-alls against the listed specifics is uncertain. The extension is also left to whatever the Architect "may determine."

This says "the Contract Sum is stated in the Agreement," but the Agreement states no sum: 5.1.1 defines it as the Cost of the Work plus the Fee and 5.2.1 fills the Guaranteed Maximum Price in as "N/A." The total amount payable is nowhere stated.

This schedule-of-values provision requires allocation of the Contract Sum, while Subparagraph 12.1.5 of the Agreement requires allocation of "the entire Guaranteed Maximum Price," which is stated as "N/A." The two allocation bases differ.

The grounds for withholding certification end with ".7 persistent failure to carry out the Work in accordance with the Contract Documents," an open-ended ground standing after six specific ones. What counts as persistent failure, and whether the list is exhaustive, is left to construction.

Payment is due "within the time provided in the Contract Documents," but Subparagraph 12.1.3 of the Agreement states that time only by reference to blanks whose figures are not legible in the executed document. The due date cannot be fixed by reading the two together.

The clause says payments "shall be held by the Contractor" for Subcontractors yet immediately disclaims any separate account, fiduciary liability or tort liability for breach of trust. Whether it creates an enforceable trust at all is a question the words themselves raise.

The right to stop work arises if the Owner does not pay "within seven days after the date established in the Contract Documents," but Subparagraph 12.1.3 of the Agreement fixes that date only through blanks that are not legible. The trigger for this remedy cannot be located in the instrument.

Substantial Completion is defined as the stage when the Work is "sufficiently complete in accordance with the Contract Documents so that the Owner can occupy or utilize the Work for its intended use," a standard with no objective measure. On a residence with a fixed completion date, whether and when that stage was reached is exactly what parties litigate.

Final payment waives the Owner's Claims except those "arising from" three listed categories, including "failure of the Work to comply with the requirements of the Contract Documents" — an exception broad enough to swallow much of the waiver. How much survives final payment is a construction question.

Acceptance of final payment waives all Claims "except those previously made in writing and identified by that payee as unsettled at the time of final Application for Payment," and neither the required form nor the timing of that identification is specified. Whether a contractor's outstanding claims survive payment turns on this sentence.

Emergency compensation is left to Paragraph 4.3 and Article 7, while the Addendum's revised 7.7.2 excludes emergency costs caused by the Contractor or preventable by timely notice. Whether an emergency claim is governed by the general or the revised cost provision is unresolved.

Coverage must be "not less than limits of liability specified in the Contract Documents or required by law, whichever coverage is greater," yet no insurance limits are stated anywhere in the Agreement, Addendum, Supplementary Conditions or Exhibits. The obligation has no figure attached to it.

The Owner need only maintain "the Owner's usual liability insurance," a standard defined solely by the Owner's own past practice. The scope and limits of the obligation cannot be determined from the words.

Whether this optional Project Management Protective Liability insurance was required matters directly to Subparagraph 3.18.1, whose indemnity applies only "to the extent claims, damages, losses or expenses are not covered" by such insurance. Nothing in the instrument says whether the Owner exercised the option.

The mutual waiver runs to damages "to the extent covered by property insurance obtained pursuant to this Paragraph 11.4 or other property insurance applicable to the Work," and the reach of "other property insurance applicable to the Work" is undefined. Whether a particular loss falls inside the waiver is the standard fight over this clause.

The one-year correction period, the Owner's duty to give notice "promptly after discovery," and the waiver of the right to require correction if the Owner fails to notify are run together in text that is partly illegible here. Whether the one-year period limits the Owner's remedies or only the duty to correct is left open.

The extension rule for Work first performed after Substantial Completion is incomplete on its face — the period by which the year is extended is missing from the sentence. The provision cannot be applied as written.

As it appears the sentence reads "the one-year period for correction of Work shall not be performed by the Contractor pursuant to this Paragraph 12.2," which is not a coherent proposition; the words fixing whether the period is extended by corrective work are missing. The rule it states is unreadable.

The assignment restriction survives only in broken form — the words prohibiting assignment of "the Contract as a whole without written consent of the other" and the consequence of an assignment without consent are partly missing. What is forbidden, and with what effect, cannot be read from the text.

The clause fixes contractual accrual dates for "any applicable statute of limitations" at Substantial Completion, issuance of the final Certificate, or the act complained of, which may not match the statutory rule. When a claim accrues, and whether the parties can fix it by agreement, are both raised by these words.

The threshold — suspensions or interruptions constituting "in the aggregate more than 100 percent of the total number of days scheduled for completion, or 120 days in any 365-day period, whichever is less" — is expressed in terms that are difficult to apply and partly garbled here. When the right to terminate arises cannot be computed with confidence.

Recovery on termination here includes "reasonable overhead, profit and damages," while Subparagraph 4.3.10 waives consequential damages expressly including damages "due to either party's termination in accordance with Article 14," and Article 13.1 of the Agreement caps what may be paid under 14.1.3. The three provisions give different measures of the same recovery.

Termination depends on the Owner having "persistently failed to fulfill the Owner's obligations under the Contract Documents with respect to matters important to the progress of the Work," with neither "persistently" nor "matters important" defined. That is the phrase on which a wrongful-termination dispute would turn.

The three specific grounds for termination are followed by ".4 otherwise is guilty of substantial breach of a provision of the Contract Documents," a general catch-all whose reach against the enumerated specifics is uncertain. "Substantial breach" is itself undefined.

The reconciliation is computed from "the unpaid balance of the Contract Sum," while Article 13.2 of the Agreement provides its own formula for termination-for-cause payment capped by the Guaranteed Maximum Price, which is stated as "N/A." The two computations of the same amount do not correspond.

Payment on convenience termination includes "reasonable overhead and profit on the Work not executed," whereas Article 13.1 of the Agreement caps amounts on a convenience termination by reference to 14.1.3 and the 13.2 formula, and 4.3.10 waives consequential damages on termination. The instrument gives conflicting measures of convenience-termination recovery.
